summary: This bill amends the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act to require states to eliminate civil and criminal statutes of limitations for child sexual abuse, exploitation, and trafficking cases and revive time-barred claims, while authorizing $20 million per year in grants through 2033 to reward states that enact one or more of these reforms.

scores.thoughts: The bill authorizes $20 million annually in grants (FY2026–2033) to states that eliminate statutes of limitations for child sexual abuse cases. This constitutes new federal spending, directly expanding government outlays.
The bill contains no provisions related to taxes, tax rates, or revenue policy.
While the grants flow through HHS, the bill addresses statutes of limitations and civil claims for child sexual abuse rather than healthcare delivery, coverage, or markets.
No provisions address firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border enforcement, or immigrant protections.
No provisions address abortion access, restrictions, or reproductive rights.
No provisions address military, defense, or national security spending.
No provisions address environmental regulations, climate policy, or natural resources.

The bill expands funding under the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act for states adopting certain reforms. This modestly increases federal support for child welfare services, a component of the social safety net.
The bill was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, but its substance concerns statutes of limitations under CAPTA and has no direct bearing on schools, funding, or education policy.
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or controlled substances.

The core purpose is to eliminate civil and criminal statutes of limitations for child sexual abuse and revive time-barred claims, enabling more prosecutions and civil suits. This strengthens enforcement and accountability for serious crimes.
No provisions address trade, tariffs, or international commerce.
By authorizing new grant spending, the bill increases federal outlays and therefore works against prioritizing debt reduction.
No provisions address LGBTQ+ legal protections or related civil rights.
No provisions address foreign aid or international assistance.
No provisions address voting rights, election procedures, or voter access.
No provisions address technology regulation, data privacy, or surveillance.
No provisions address labor law, unions, or worker/employer relations.
No provisions address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination protections.
